Position authority varies greatly: budget limits, contract signing, personnel decisions, and supplier selection rights belong to different roles in different organizations, and no single checklist item can replace verification of the actual authority of the target position.

Use the fictional facilities task in A1–A5 to observe yourself: whether you can rank three on-site exceptions by priority, verify the contractor's scope and amounts item by item, and, after the conditions in A4 change, preserve the unknowns and escalate to the authorized person in A5. The exercise is only for understanding whether you are willing to repeatedly verify on-site facts, maintenance records, supplier delivery, and authority boundaries over the long term, not a suitability score or a hiring judgment.

The more telling signal is this: you are willing to handle an interrupted daily routine, can turn vague complaints into observable problems, and accept that your results mostly show up as other people's work going smoothly. Signals for caution are acting only when requirements are fully specified, or being in an organization that makes you responsible for costs without giving you the corresponding approval and inquiry authority; the latter should have its boundaries clarified before starting.

The conclusions on this card come from public occupational task materials and editorial summary, not from an individual assessment of you, and they do not predict employment outcomes. A facilities manager's actual authority depends on organization size, the authorization system, and internal control requirements; the same English title may correspond to a completely different scope of work at different companies.

If you are willing to handle the long chain of facilities operations support chores over the long term, investigate service interruptions and push for restoration, and keep reviewable records for all of it, this work is worth learning more about. When judging a position, first ask three things: how much budget, how far can you approve, and whom do you escalate to when something goes wrong.

Facilities managers organize work around the operation and maintenance of buildings, grounds, equipment, and materials, and oversee repairs, projects, budgets, and space arrangements. The following is an editorial overview of the task organization: verify on-site facts and priorities, coordinate contractors, track delivery and costs, record open items, and escalate per authority; actual processes and professional sign-off authority are verified by the institution.

entries: Demand triage｜Receive repair, operations, and space requests and set maintenance priorities by safety, business impact, and time limit.｜Output a work order with facts, unknowns, interim measures, and escalation deadlines.

Maintenance planning｜Turn equipment condition, preventive maintenance windows, and user constraints into an executable schedule.｜Output the plan version, shutdown windows, responsible persons, and re-check points.

Contractor delivery｜Verify the scope of service, quotes, site permits, and professional qualifications, organize the work, and collect test evidence.｜Output scope comparisons, work orders, photos, test results, and acceptance records.

Costs and changes｜Track budgets, contract scope, interim measures, and change requests.｜Output auditable amount calculations, variance explanations, and pending approval items; do not substitute for payment or contract approval.

Safety and continuity｜Identify fire, electrical, structural, environmental, and critical facility risks and coordinate closures, alternate routes, or shutdowns.｜Output a risk escalation form; professional safety conclusions go to the responsible person with the qualifications and authority.

Handover and review｜Hand the site status, supplier commitments, open issues, and follow-up checks to the next responsible person.｜Output a handover record with version, status, evidence location, and deadline.

You are the facilities manager of the fictional Qinghe Campus and are responsible for operations support of an office building of about 2,000 square meters. The amounts, dates, roles, and on-site phenomena below are exercise settings, not on-site records, real quotes, or safety instructions.

A1｜2026-09-14: First, 08:10, the west third-floor air conditioning unit alarmed and the temperature in two rooms kept rising; record the alarm information, notify users, and contact a certified technician, and the root cause and electrical safety status are pending confirmation. Second, 08:25, a fire escape light in the east stairwell flickered; the on-site safety manager approved closing the affected short section first and activating the backup route, to be executed by the corresponding on-site personnel, and the backup lighting and battery status are pending professional confirmation. Third, 08:40, after the rain, a wet mark of about 2 meters appeared on the meeting room ceiling; equipment was moved away and a drip tray placed, no collapse was seen, but the leak source and structural damage are pending confirmation by the building contractor.

A2｜Contractor A: available on 2026-09-14 from 13:00 to 17:00; the scope is three preliminary inspections, replacement of one light fixture, and temporary leak protection; labor 4,800 yuan and materials 1,200 yuan, totaling 6,000 yuan (taxes not stated). Includes inspection records, on-site photos, a material list, and functional testing; excludes roof waterproofing repair and electrical distribution box work; acceptance evidence is test results, photos, and signatures on both parties' work orders.

A3｜Contractor B: available on 2026-09-15 from 08:00 to 12:00; can do the air conditioning inspection and light fixture replacement, with roof assessment only and no repair; labor 5,500 yuan and materials up to 800 yuan, for a total ceiling of 6,300 yuan, but taxes and travel costs are not stated. The light fixture warranty is 30 days; excludes night work and waterproofing repair; qualification documents have not yet been provided, and whether a photo package, weekend response, and distribution box work are included is unknown.

A4｜2026-09-14 11:30: a new round of rain expanded the meeting room wet mark to about 4 meters, there is an external meeting at 15:00, and the earlier condition that assessment could wait until the next day has changed; equipment must be protected first, whether to close the meeting room must be confirmed, and the contractor's arrival and temporary leak protection capability must be re-verified.

A5｜Roles and authority: facilities manager Lin Qiao organizes recommendations and keeps records; the office administration team is the affected user; the budget ceiling is 6,500 yuan (pre-tax); finance lead Zhou Lan approves over-budget spending and payments; the on-site safety manager approves shutdowns or closures; certified technicians confirm electrical, fire, and structural matters. If the safety status is unclear, the expected shutdown exceeds 30 minutes, or the total may exceed 6,500 yuan, escalate immediately and require the relevant responsible persons to reply within 30 minutes.

Read the brief and A1/A5 and write a role boundary card: what may be recorded and temporarily coordinated, what requires approval for budget, shutdown, or closure, and what is prohibited such as signing on others' behalf or making professional safety judgments, one column each.
Day two

Read A1 and fill in the priority table for the three incidents, writing the time, impact, interim measures, and items pending professional confirmation for each; check that observations are not written as safety conclusions.
Day three
Read A2/A3 and calculate the ceilings of 4,800+1,200=6,000 yuan and 5,500+800=6,300 yuan; list A's taxes and B's taxes, travel, and qualifications as unknown.
Day four

Read A4 and fill in the exception escalation form, explaining that the wet mark expanded from about 2 meters to about 4 meters, the impact on the 15:00 meeting, optional interim measures, and the approval request; do not promise that the contractor will definitely arrive.
Day five
Per A1–A5, consolidate the quotes, priorities, open questions, responsible persons, and next steps into a handover record; check each item back against the original text.
Day six
Seal the initial draft first, then open the reference approach and compare priorities, calculations, unknowns, and authorization boundaries, listing omissions and reasons for revision.
Day seven

Reread the initial and revised drafts and fill in the review: omissions, explanation of changes, basis for revisions, and subjective energy; do not calculate a suitability score or treat the exercise results as a hiring conclusion.

items.title: Seven-day experience: complete one facilities operations support loop with fictional materials

entries: Keep the initial and revised drafts and record item by item as which A1–A5 material was missed, the earlier explanation, the current explanation, and the basis for revision.

Do the priority and quote comparison table again and compare whether omissions decreased and whether unknowns are still preserved.
If you still are not clear whether you like this kind of work after finishing, list the recurring difficulties as specific questions for the next round of learning about facilities manager work.
